episode_summary: Hashing It Out episode 92, recorded in September 2020, with Rex Hygate, founder of DefiSafety. He explains DefiSafety's process quality audit and the DeFi Safety score: a public-information-only, four-section questionnaire rated red, yellow or green. The hosts and Rex discuss the audit's turnaround and price, how developers respond, audits used as marketing, private repositories, the limits of a score, funding by users rather than developers, and planned version 0.6 changes.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said he started looking at Ethereum right after the DAO hack and only lurked at first.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: So I actually started looking at Ethereum right after the DAO, which was really cool. And I just lurked.

cards.claim: In 2018 Rex Hygate met Bryant at a hackathon in Denver and they started securef.org, focused on software process and documentation for blockchain software.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: And there I met Bryant and we started securef.org, which was focused on software process and documentation for making blockchain software.

cards.claim: Rex Hygate said he created the DeFi safety score by taking the testing, coding and documentation process from securef and adapting it into a DeFi safety audit.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: So I took the roots of the concept of Secureth, looking at the testing process and the coding process and the documentation process. And from that, I came up with the idea of a DeFi safety score

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said DeFi Safety had gone live in July and had completed 23 audits.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: and I invented the process and in July we went live and I think we've got 23 audits completed now.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said DeFi Safety audits only use publicly available information such as the website, GitHub and Medium articles.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I only look at publicly available audits or publicly available information.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said most DeFi developers did not yet trace software requirements to code and tests, which he called a real aerospace-style practice.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: can you trace from the software from the requirements to the code and to the test like did they put in traceability and that's something that i would say most people don't do yet

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said a DeFi Safety audit would cost under $5K and usually take about a week.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: It will be under 5K and generally results can be done in about a week

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said every question in a DeFi Safety report is paired with guidance on how to improve the score.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: In fact, underneath every question in the report is how to improve the score.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said DeFi Safety scored each question on a fixed percentage rubric, such as 100 for an audit before deployment.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: a hundred percent means this zero percent means this forty percent means this sixty percent means this

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said a project that claims an audit it cannot show should score zero, since such claims are sometimes invalid.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: is 20 zero percent is saying you have an audit when you don't really

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said DeFi Safety would not give scores to projects whose code or audits were not public.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I audit public things. If it's not public, I'm not going to give scores on it.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said he had committed to releasing version 0.6 of the DeFi Safety process.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: And actually, I'm at version 0.5 of my process. I've committed that I'm going to do 0.6.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said a lot of DeFi projects were moving to private repositories because they were afraid of getting forked.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: a lot of people are having private repositories because they're afraid of getting forked.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said Aave kept its development in a private GitLab and published releases to stop people taking the code before launch.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: the purpose for that is so that people can't take the code before they release it

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said he was getting one or two audit requests a day from users, many of them repeats.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I'm getting one or two requests a day from users. A lot of them are repeats.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said DeFi Safety was not yet charging for audits but expected to start offering paid audits to skip the line.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: And at this point, I'm not really charging, but I think I'm getting into the field where I will be offering four charge audits for people to, you know, sort of skip the line.

cards.claim: In 2020 Rex Hygate said one of his early audits of Aave took a long time because he could not find where its smart contract addresses were listed.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: one of my early audits was ave and i never found where they had their smart contract addresses so that was a huge thing

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said a DeFi project with anonymous developers and no published contracts or GitHub is a giant red flag.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: Because if you're capable of creating smart contracts that do the complex things that keep up with the other programs, then you know what's going on.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said he reads the audit reports himself, giving projects benefit of the doubt but checking whether bugs were actually fixed.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: So when I look at the audits, I actually do read the audits. And I am not a smart contract auditor, but I'm pretty good on quality.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said an audit that was all bad and was done after deployment with no changes would be a giant red flag for him.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: the audit was all bad and there's no you know say it was audited after deployment and there were no changes, that would be a giant red flag for me.

cards.claim: In 2020 Rex Hygate said projects pointed to audits as cover after hacks, but when people read the auditor's report it often said bad things.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: And inevitably, people actually look at the audit and they're like, oh, it didn't actually, the auditor didn't even say very good things about it.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said DeFi Safety was paid by the developers it rated, which created pressure to stay quiet about risks.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: Because frankly, we get paid by the developer, right? And if I'm really brutal in my language,

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said it was not his job to tell people whether to invest, and that doing so could cause trouble if the call was wrong.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: like it's not my job to say do or do not put money in this. And if we start doing that, we're gonna get trouble

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said he wanted DeFi Safety funded by users for users, not by developers, and said it was too early to know how.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I want it to be funded by the users, independent of the developers, funded by the users giving information for the users.

cards.claim: Rex Hygate said in September 2020 that the 2008 credit rating agencies had a system where issuers paid for their own ratings, which became corrupt over time.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: You go back, you look at the rating agencies in 2008. You know, you had a perfectly good system where the ratings were paid for by the people who were getting the ratings.

cards.claim: In 2020 Rex Hygate said he audited BZX v1 after its first hack to test whether his process would raise red flags, and it did.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I actually audited BZX v1 after their first hack just to see whether or not my process would bring up any red flags.

cards.claim: In 2020 Rex Hygate said OPEN had been hacked but still received a really good DeFi Safety score in his audit.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: And it did. And then I audited OPEN, which had a hack, and they got a really good score.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said a DeFi Safety score cannot detect dishonest incentives because the process does not read or review the code's behaviour.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I don't read the code. I don't go over what the code does. So that's a huge hole.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said a developer who has honest work but dishonest incentives would not be caught by a DeFi Safety score.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: So if somebody's done honest work but has dishonest incentives, I won't catch that.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said he checked test presence and test-to-code ratios rather than running the tests himself.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I only look at tests. Oh, look, he has lots of tests. And, you know, I can do a test to code ratio.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said finding the GitHub repository matching the code on mainnet was one of his biggest technical challenges.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: frequently one of my biggest technical challenges is just trying to find the the github repository that matches the code on the mainnet

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said a DeFi Safety score could be shown in a wallet when a user connects to an app or confirms a transaction.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: you can actually display that on the wallet when you're connecting to an app and when you're about to do a confirm.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said every DeFi project should have a security page answering the DeFi Safety questions so it could self-score.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I think every project should have a like slash security page. You know, if they have a bounty, that's where all the information should be about their bounty, their contact information.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate predicted that DeFi auditing would become a quality industry with standard processes as the field grew.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: the idea this is it'll become a quality industry at a certain point as this grows with lots of people involved in it.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said he had read there were around 30,000 DeFi deployments a month, up from about 50.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: I think I read that there were, what, 30,000 deployments a month now, which is insane, where it used to be like 50.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said he planned to add a risk metric that measures total value locked over time, where a bigger area under the curve means a safer protocol.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: you look at total value over time, and you take the area of the curve, and the bigger that is, the safer it is the time without hacks or whatever.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said he ran the SCC code-counting tool on core contracts to get lines of code, comments and a complexity figure.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: And I run a tool called SCC on it, which gives, you know, the number of lines, number of comments and a generic code complexity thing

cards.claim: In September 2020 a host asked what DeFi Safety would do if a user offered to pay for a worse score.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: Now, what do you do when a user says, like, find the problem with this shit project, and I'll pay you more if you give it a worse score?

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said credibility was the only thing DeFi Safety had going for it, so bribes for a worse score would be expensive to accept.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: on something like this, credibility is the only thing you've got going for you.

cards.claim: In September 2020 Rex Hygate said DeFi Safety screenshots public web pages and links them in reports so later changes can be compared to what was seen.
cards.speaker: guest
cards.quote: And with websites, I try to do a screen cap and then put it in there with the link. So if it changes a week later, I can at least say this is what I saw when I did it.

title: DefiSafety - Rex Hygate
